questions.p: Grace, 48, has a 1.4 cm breast carcinoma excised with sentinel node biopsy. The report reads poorly differentiated invasive ductal carcinoma, 0 of 3 lymph nodes positive. Staging CT shows no distant spread. Which statement best describes her tumour?
o: Advanced stage with an aggressive, high grade
Early stage with an aggressive, high grade
Early stage with an indolent, low grade
Advanced stage with an indolent, low grade
questions.e:
B is correct. Stage describes size and spread. A small tumour with N0 and M0 is early stage. Grade describes how cells look. Poorly differentiated is grade III, aggressive.
A: Grade is right, but N0 M0 at 1.4 cm is not advanced.
C: The stage is right, but poorly differentiated cells are high grade.
D: No nodes or metastases rules out advanced stage, and poor differentiation rules out low grade.
High yield: Grade and stage are separate. Both inform prognosis and treatment.

questions.p: Two families attend a cancer genetics clinic. In Family 1, a single activating mutation in one allele of RET drives medullary thyroid cancer. In Family 2, a child inherits one mutated Rb allele and develops cancer after a second mutation. Which classification of each gene is correct, in order?
o: Oncogene in both of the two families
Tumour suppressor in both of the families
questions.e:
C is correct. RET is a proto-oncogene, and a single hit in one allele makes it an oncogene (gain of function). Rb is a tumour suppressor gene that needs two hits (loss of function), and an inherited first hit raises risk.
A: Rb needs two hits, the hallmark of a tumour suppressor.
B: RET needs only one hit, the hallmark of an oncogene.
D: This reverses the two mechanisms.
High yield: One hit: Ras, c-myc, Her2-neu, RET. Two hits: p53, Rb, PTEN, BRCA1/2.

questions.p: Ahmed, 47, grew up in rural Egypt and had a parasitic infection as a child that was never treated. He now has painless blood in his urine, and cystoscopy shows a bladder mass. Which organism most likely contributed to his cancer?
questions.e:
D is correct. Schistosoma (blood flukes) is linked to bladder cancer.
A: H. pylori causes gastric cancer.
B: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell lymphoma.
C: The Southeast Asian liver fluke causes cholangiocarcinoma.
High yield: HPV: cervical, anal, oropharyngeal. HBV and HCV: hepatocellular. EBV: nasopharyngeal, Burkitt, Hodgkin. HHV8: Kaposi sarcoma.

questions.p: A cervical biopsy from Mei, 33, shows dysplastic cells spanning the full thickness of the squamous epithelium. The basement membrane is intact throughout and no dysplastic cells are seen beneath it. Which term and implication fit best?
o: Carcinoma in situ, not yet a malignant neoplasm
Invasive carcinoma, at risk of nodal spread
Metastasis, spread from a distant primary
questions.e:
A is correct. Dysplastic cells involving the entire epithelial thickness and pushing against an intact basement membrane define carcinoma in situ (high grade dysplasia), which is pre-malignant.
B: A malignant neoplasm needs cells past the basement membrane.
C: Metaplasia is a change of cell type without dysplasia.
D: Metastasis is spread to and invasion of other tissues.
High yield: Pap testing screens for this pre-cancer stage.

questions.p: Chloe, 24, notices a new lump in her left breast. On exam there is a 2 cm smooth, firm, mobile, non-tender mass with no skin or nipple changes and no palpable axillary nodes. Which is the most appropriate first imaging test?
questions.e:
A is correct. Ultrasound is the first modality for a palpable lump and for women under 30.
B: CT is for staging after biopsy and is not used in the workup.
C: MRI is for high-risk screening, high breast density and local staging.
D: Mammography is not the first modality for a palpable lump in a woman under 30.
High yield: Firm, mobile, well-circumscribed fits fibroadenoma, a benign neoplasm.

questions.p: Hannah, 32, tested positive for a pathogenic BRCA1 variant after her mother's ovarian cancer diagnosis. She has no breast symptoms and a normal clinical breast exam. Which breast screening plan fits?
o: Annual MRI and mammogram, from now
questions.e:
C is correct. BRCA carriers have an annual mammogram from 30 and breast MRI from 30 to 69. She is 32, so screening applies now.
A: Mammogram alone misses MRI, and 40 is too late.
B: Every 2 years from 50 is the average-risk program.
D: Clinical exams alone are not the plan. Age 35 is the BRCA1 prophylactic surgery milestone.
High yield: Prophylactic surgery: age 35 for BRCA1, age 40 for BRCA2.

questions.p: Ruth, 66, has a breast mass that radiology rates as highly suspicious for malignancy. Her core needle biopsy returns as benign breast tissue. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure her and return to routine screening
Repeat a screening mammogram in 2 years
Discuss the discordance with the pathologist
Refer for mastectomy without further review
questions.e:
C is correct. Clinical-pathological non-concordance is a reason to communicate directly, beyond the requisition.
A: Reassurance ignores imaging and pathology that disagree.
B: Routine interval screening ignores a suspicious lesion.
D: Surgery skips resolving the discordance.
High yield: Other triggers: unusual or ambiguous result, missing information, rare diagnosis, urgent result needed.

questions.p: Three patients attend a breast cancer clinic. Patient 1 receives chemotherapy before surgery to shrink a 6 cm tumour. Patient 2 receives radiation after surgery for micro-metastatic disease. Patient 3 receives radiation to relieve pain from a spinal metastasis. Which intent applies to each, in order?
questions.e:
B is correct. Before surgery to shrink a tumour is neoadjuvant. After surgery for micro-metastatic disease is adjuvant. Radiation to relieve symptoms of metastatic disease is palliative.
A: Patient 2 is post-surgical (adjuvant) and Patient 3 is palliative.
C: Symptom relief for a metastasis is palliative, not curative.
D: This swaps the first two.
High yield: Radiation oncology aims to reduce local recurrence or metastasis, or to relieve symptoms.

questions.p: Tamara, 41, carries a pathogenic BRCA2 variant. She asks you to order the same test for her healthy 12-year-old daughter so the family has time to plan. Which response best follows the ethics of cancer genetic testing?
o: Test only if the daughter develops breast changes
Defer testing until she is an adult and chooses
Test now, since results will guide her screening
Test now, since a parent holds full decision rights
questions.e:
B is correct. Avoid testing children for adult-onset conditions because of stigmatization, anxiety and vulnerable child parenting. Autonomy makes testing each person's own choice.
A: Symptoms call for diagnostic workup, not predictive testing of a minor.
C: BRCA surveillance starts at 30, so a result guides nothing in childhood.
D: The decision belongs to the person tested, under autonomy.
High yield: Confirm a mutation in an affected relative before testing unaffected relatives.

questions.p: Jonah, 39, tests positive for a pathogenic variant causing Lynch syndrome. He does not want his sister told, citing a long family conflict. Which approach best reflects the ethics of sharing genetic results?
o: Contact his sister directly, since beneficence wins
Insist results be shared with all first-degree relatives
Withhold further counselling until he agrees to share
Respect his choice and explain the benefit to relatives
questions.e:
D is correct. Under autonomy, it is the patient's right to choose who knows his results. Beneficence supports explaining that relatives have the option of surveillance.
A: Disclosure without consent violates his autonomy.
B: No rule makes sharing mandatory.
C: Withholding counselling breaches non-maleficence and justice.
High yield: Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice all apply to genetic testing.

questions.p:
Regarding cancer statistics in Canada, which of the following statements are true?
i) Colorectal cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death
ii) Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in women
iii) About 1 in 2 Canadians will develop cancer in their lifetime
iv) Prostate cancer is the most often diagnosed cancer overall
questions.e:
D is correct. Canadian cancer mortality ranks lung, colorectum, then pancreas. 1 in 2 Canadians develop cancer and 1 in 4 die of it.
A: Lung leads cancer deaths in women. Breast is second.
B: Statements ii and iv are both false.
C: Lung is the most diagnosed cancer overall. Prostate is first in men only.
E: Statements ii and iv are false.
High yield: High-income countries have higher incidence and lower mortality.

questions.p: You meet Mr. Laurent, 70, to discuss biopsy results confirming metastatic pancreatic cancer. When you ask what he understands so far, he says the scan showed a cyst and he expects to be back at work next week. Within SPIKES, which step are you in, and what is the best approach?
o: Perception, do not confront his denial at this visit
Knowledge, correct his understanding with all details
Empathy, name his emotion before checking understanding
Invitation, ask permission before sharing information
questions.e:
A is correct. Asking what he knows before you tell is Perception. If a patient is in denial, do not confront the denial at the first interview.
B: Knowledge comes later, with a warning, no jargon and small chunks.
C: Empathy responds to emotions as they arise after news is given.
D: Invitation follows Perception and asks how much he wants to know.
High yield: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy and summary.

questions.p: Doug, 63, smoked for decades and has a 45 pack-year history. He quit 18 years ago. He feels well and has no symptoms. He asks about lung cancer screening. Which response is correct?
o: He qualifies for a screening chest X-ray each year
He qualifies for annual low-dose CT, up to 3 times
He is not eligible, since he quit over 15 years ago
He qualifies, since pack-years alone define eligibility
questions.e:
C is correct. Lung screening covers adults 55-74 with a 30 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit less than 15 years ago. Quitting 18 years ago excludes him.
A: CXR is not ordered for routine screening.
B: He meets age and pack-years but fails the quit-time criterion.
D: Eligibility needs age, pack-years and quit time together.
High yield: Check every criterion, not only the most striking one.

questions.p: Lena, 58, has metastatic breast cancer. Over one week she has had back pain, and now both legs are weak with brisk reflexes and upgoing plantar responses. Her arms are normal. Which cancer emergency is most likely?
questions.e:
B is correct. UMN signs in both legs with normal arms (paraparesis) localize to the thoracic cord. In a patient with cancer this fits spinal cord compression, a listed cancer emergency.
A: SVC obstruction does not cause leg weakness with UMN signs.
C: Hypercalcemia does not produce a cord-level UMN pattern.
D: A brain lesion gives a hemibody pattern, not weakness of both legs with normal arms.
High yield: Life-threatening: metastases compressing the spinal cord or major vessels.

questions.p: Priya, 34, reports lumpy, nodular breasts on both sides. The lumps become tender in the days before her period and settle afterward. Exam shows no dominant mass, skin change or nipple change. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.e:
A is correct. Fibrocystic change gives lumpy, nodular breasts with pain and tenderness that varies through the menstrual cycle.
B: An abscess is a collection of pus from bacterial infection, with acute inflammation.
C: A fibroadenoma is a single, well-circumscribed, firm, mobile nodule.
D: A cyst is a single sac that collapses when fluid is removed.
High yield: VITAMIN C&D for a breast mass: infection, trauma, neoplasm, cyst.

questions.p: Dana, 45, had a car accident 3 weeks ago and still has a seatbelt bruise across her chest. She now feels a firm lump in the breast under the bruise. Using the VITAMIN C&D approach, which cause best fits?
questions.e:
C is correct. The trauma category of VITAMIN C&D for a breast mass is fat necrosis. The recent blunt injury at the same site is the clue.
A: Fibrocystic change varies with the menstrual cycle.
B: An abscess follows infection, with acute inflammation.
D: A fibroadenoma is a benign neoplasm unrelated to injury.
High yield: Increasing age raises the likelihood of cancer, so a persistent mass still needs workup.

questions.p: A family physician is building a workup for a new palpable breast mass in a 52-year-old. Which investigation has no role in diagnosing the type of breast mass?
questions.e:
B is correct. No blood or urine test helps identify the type of breast mass, so lab medicine has no role in diagnosis.
A: Mammography is used in screening and diagnosis.
C: Biopsy under ultrasound or stereotactic guidance gives the tissue diagnosis.
D: Ultrasound is a primary diagnostic tool for a palpable lump.
High yield: Your Week 6 quiz listed tumour markers as a distractor for the same reason.

questions.p: A surgeon completes the pathology requisition for a lumpectomy specimen. Which item belongs on the requisition rather than in the pathology report?
o: The ACMG classification of a variant
The time the specimen went into formalin
The synoptic summary of the margins
The ER, PR and Her2 biomarker test results
questions.e:
B is correct. The requisition carries patient ID, ischemic time, date and time of procurement and formalin, exact sites and clinical information.
A: ACMG classification appears in the cancer genetic report.
C: The synoptic report is part of the microscopic description in the pathology report.
D: ER, PR and Her2 results appear in the pathology report.
High yield: Clinical information on the requisition: history, imaging, reason for test, DDx, pitfalls, ancillary tests.

questions.p: Four core biopsy reports use different phrases. Which phrase signals the greatest concern for cancer while stopping short of a definite malignant diagnosis?
questions.e:
C is correct. The narrative scale runs: positive, suspicious, atypia that cannot exclude malignancy, atypia favouring reactive, negative. Suspicious sits directly below positive.
A: This sits one step below suspicious.
B: This leans toward a benign, reactive process.
D: This rules out malignancy.
High yield: An ambiguous result is a reason to talk to the pathologist directly.

questions.p: Helen, 44, has a hereditary cancer panel. The report lists one variant with an ACMG classification of 3. How should this result be described to her?
o: A likely pathogenic variant that raises risk
questions.e:
A is correct. ACMG classes: 1 pathogenic, 2 likely pathogenic, 3 VUS, 4 likely benign, 5 benign.
B: Pathogenic is class 1.
C: Likely pathogenic is class 2.
D: Likely benign is class 4.
High yield: The panel tests 37 genes on a blood sample.

questions.p:
Regarding the drawbacks of cancer genetic testing, which of the following statements are true?
i) Results include false positives and false negatives
ii) Current tests identify all inherited gene changes linked to cancer
iii) Effective risk reduction or early detection methods might not exist
iv) A positive result often leads to more worry, appointments and tests
questions.e:
A is correct. Drawbacks include false results, tests that miss some inherited changes, a lack of effective risk reduction for some cancers, and more worry and procedures after a positive result.
B: Statement iii is also true.
C: Statement ii is false.
D: Statement ii is false and iv is true.
E: Statement ii is false.
High yield: Benefits: better risk prediction, relief of uncertainty, testing options for relatives, earlier detection.

questions.p: In culture, cells from a patient's tumour keep dividing well past 70 divisions without stopping, and their telomeres stay long. Which hallmark of cancer does this show?
questions.e:
C is correct. Cancer cells produce telomerase, which lengthens telomeres and overcomes the Hayflick limit of 60-70 divisions.
A: Self-sufficiency involves making their own growth factors and always-on receptors.
B: Sustained angiogenesis involves the angiogenic switch.
D: Evasion of apoptosis most often involves p53 mutations.
High yield: Emerging hallmarks: immune evasion, tumour-promoting inflammation, genome instability, deregulated energetics.

questions.p: In the two stage clonal expansion model, a genetic alteration has produced premalignant cells, and these cells are now proliferating. Which stage comes next?
questions.e:
D is correct. The model runs initiation, promotion, transformation, then progression. After premalignant cells proliferate (promotion), a second rapid alteration produces a malignant cell (transformation).
A: The angiogenic switch is a hallmark of cancer, not a stage of this model.
B: Initiation already happened when the premalignant cell formed.
C: Progression follows transformation, from malignant cell to clinical cancer.
High yield: Cancer is usually a cascade of mutations, not one.

questions.p: During a breast cancer risk review, two factors are noted for Amira, 47: early menarche and never breastfeeding, and then regular tanning bed use. How is each risk factor classified, in order?
o: Modifiable in both of the cases
Non-modifiable in both of the cases
questions.e:
B is correct. Reproductive history (breastfeeding, menarche, menopause) is a non-modifiable factor in GGRAPES. Tanning beds are a modifiable factor.
A: Reproductive history is non-modifiable.
C: Tanning bed use is modifiable.
D: This reverses the two.
High yield: GGRAPES: geography, genetic susceptibility, reproductive history, age, precursor lesions, ethnicity, sex.

questions.p: An Indigenous patient with a strong family history of breast cancer meets two team members. Member 1 does her risk assessment, takes informed consent for genetic testing and plans screening of her relatives. Member 2 helps her navigate the health care system and provides counselling. Who are they, in order?
o: Genetics counsellor, then Indigenous health navigator
Primary care physician, then palliative care physician
questions.e:
A is correct. The genetics counsellor does risk assessment, consent for genetic testing and screening of family members. The Indigenous health navigator advocates by helping navigate the health care system, plus counselling.
B: The medical oncologist gives systemic therapies.
C: Primary care does screening, symptom relief and referrals. Palliative care relieves suffering.
D: The social worker helps navigate the journey to recovery, and does not take consent for genetic testing.
High yield: Gynecological surgeon: fertility and pregnancy options, prophylactic surgery.

questions.p: A staging report reads T2 N1 M1. The N and M categories each describe a route of cancer spread. Which routes do they capture, in order?
questions.e:
D is correct. T reflects direct local growth, N reflects lymphatic spread to regional nodes, and M reflects hematogenous metastasis.
A: This reverses the two.
B: M captures hematogenous spread, not direct growth.
C: Direct growth is captured by T.
High yield: M1 means stage IV: spread to at least one other organ.

questions.p: Two sections of a surgical pathology report are described. Section 1 gives the location and type of the tissue sample. Section 2 is the overall summary of the most important findings and influences management. Which sections are these, in order?
questions.e:
A is correct. The Specimen section gives the location and type of tissue. The Diagnosis section is the overall summary of the most important findings, and it influences management.
B: Clinical information carries the history from the requisition.
C: The synoptic report is a checklist, not the overall summary.
D: The gross description covers the specimen's appearance, ink and section codes. The synoptic report is the checklist within the microscopic description.
High yield: Your mock exam miss: the synoptic report is the checklist, and the Diagnosis section is the summary.

questions.p: An oncologist needs the margin status, lymph node findings and stage classification for a resected breast cancer. In which part of the pathology report are these found?
o: The gross description of the whole specimen
questions.e:
E is correct. The synoptic report, within the microscopic description, lists specimen, tumour, margins, lymph nodes, stage classification, additional findings and comments.
A: The specimen section gives location and type of tissue.
B: The Diagnosis is an overall summary, not the full checklist.
C: Clinical information comes from the requisition.
D: The gross description gives specimen, main findings, ink code and section code.
High yield: ER, PR and Her2 biomarker results also sit in the microscopic description.

questions.p: Helen's hereditary cancer genetic report is marked ABNORMAL. Which statement about this type of report is correct?
o: Its Interpretation gives significance from ClinVar
The hereditary cancer panel tests 5 genes
A variant of uncertain significance is ACMG class 2
Its specimen is tumour tissue from the biopsy site
An ACMG class 5 variant is pathogenic
questions.e:
A is correct. The Interpretation section states the result, the findings (type of mutation, exon, gene) and the clinical significance from ClinVar and the literature.
B: The multi-gene panel tests 37 genes.
C: A VUS is class 3. Class 2 is likely pathogenic.
D: The specimen is blood.
E: Class 5 is benign. Class 1 is pathogenic.
High yield: ACMG: 1 pathogenic, 2 likely pathogenic, 3 VUS, 4 likely benign, 5 benign.

questions.p: A medical student lists screening intervals for average-risk adults. Which interval is correct?
o: Prostate PSA every year from age 55
questions.e:
E is correct. Cervical screening with a Pap test is every 3 years for women 25-70.
A: FIT is every 2 years.
B: Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy is every 10 years.
C: PSA for men 55-69 is every 2-4 years.
D: Average-risk mammograms are every 2 years from 50 to 74.
High yield: Your first-try miss on the mock: sigmoidoscopy is every 10 years, not 2.

questions.p: Mrs. Leclerc, 71, is healthy and has had three negative Pap tests in a row over the last 10 years. She asks whether she still needs cervical screening. What is the best answer?
o: Continue Pap tests every 3 years for life
Continue Pap tests every 3 years until age 74
She has aged out of cervical screening
Switch to mammograms in place of Pap tests
Switch to a yearly Pap test after age 70
questions.e:
C is correct. Cervical screening runs ages 25-70. Women over 70 with 3 or more successive negative tests in the last 10 years are out.
A: Screening stops at 70 with a negative history.
B: 74 is the stop age for breast and colorectal screening, not cervical.
D: Mammograms screen for breast cancer, not cervical cancer.
E: No yearly Pap test is recommended after 70.
High yield: Stop ages: cervical 70, breast 74, colorectal 74, prostate 69.

questions.p: Mr. Becker, 74, feels well and asks his family doctor to start yearly PSA tests for prostate cancer screening. Which response fits the screening guidance?
o: He is outside the PSA group at age 70+
Order a low-dose CT scan instead
Start PSA because everyone over 55 qualifies
Start a yearly PSA with a yearly DRE
Start PSA every 2-4 years until age 80
questions.e:
A is correct. PSA screening is for men 55-69 every 2-4 years. Men 70 and over are out.
B: Low-dose CT screens for lung cancer.
C: The window is 55-69, not everyone over 55.
D: Yearly PSA and DRE from 45 is for BRCA-positive men.
E: Screening ends at 69.
High yield: Of 1,000 men tested, about 1 escapes death, which is why PSA screening is controversial.
